claim: Most mammals maintain their body temperature around 37°C.
source: Most mammals maintain their body temperature around 37°C, whereas in hibernators it can approach 0°C without triggering a thermogenic response.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about mammalian thermoregulation.

claim: In hibernators, body temperature can approach 0°C without triggering a thermogenic response.
source: Most mammals maintain their body temperature around 37°C, whereas in hibernators it can approach 0°C without triggering a thermogenic response.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hibernating mammals.

claim: The preoptic area (POA) of the hypothalamus is a critical thermoregulatory region.
source: Here we leverage the thermoregulatory differences between mice and hibernating thirteen-lined ground squirrels (Ictidomys tridecemlineatus) to investigate the mechanism of cold sensitivity in the preoptic area (POA) of the hypothalamus, a critical thermoregulatory region.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the Introduction section and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Mice have a larger proportion of cold-sensitive neurons in the POA compared to thirteen-lined ground squirrels.
source: We report that, in comparison to squirrels, mice have a larger proportion of cold-sensitive neurons in the POA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Mouse cold-sensitive POA neurons express the cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channel CNGA3.
source: We further show that mouse cold-sensitive neurons express the cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channel CNGA3, and that mouse, but not squirrel, CNGA3 is potentiated by cold.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic analysis and RNA in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Mouse CNGA3 is potentiated by cold.
source: We further show that mouse cold-sensitive neurons express the cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channel CNGA3, and that mouse, but not squirrel, CNGA3 is potentiated by cold.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in oocytes and HEK293T cells presented in Figures 4, 7, 8, and 9.

claim: Squirrel CNGA3 is not potentiated by cold.
source: We further show that mouse cold-sensitive neurons express the cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channel CNGA3, and that mouse, but not squirrel, CNGA3 is potentiated by cold.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in oocytes and HEK293T cells presented in Figures 4, 7, and 9.

claim: CNGA3 acts as a hypothalamic cold sensor.
source: Our data reveal CNGA3 as a hypothalamic cold sensor and a molecular marker to interrogate the neuronal circuitry underlying thermoregulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data showing cold potentiation of mouse CNGA3 and its expression in cold-sensitive POA neurons.

claim: CNGA3 is a molecular marker to interrogate the neuronal circuitry underlying thermoregulation.
source: Our data reveal CNGA3 as a hypothalamic cold sensor and a molecular marker to interrogate the neuronal circuitry underlying thermoregulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of CNGA3 in cold-sensitive POA neurons.

claim: The POA integrates signals from peripheral thermoreceptors.
source: It integrates signals from peripheral thermoreceptors and detects chemical cues produced by infectious agents to orchestrate physiological and behavioural thermoregulatory responses (Angilletta et al., 2019; Madden and Morrison, 2019; Siemens and Kamm, 2018; Tan and Knight, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The POA detects chemical cues produced by infectious agents.
source: It integrates signals from peripheral thermoreceptors and detects chemical cues produced by infectious agents to orchestrate physiological and behavioural thermoregulatory responses (Angilletta et al., 2019; Madden and Morrison, 2019; Siemens and Kamm, 2018; Tan and Knight, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The POA orchestrates physiological and behavioural thermoregulatory responses.
source: It integrates signals from peripheral thermoreceptors and detects chemical cues produced by infectious agents to orchestrate physiological and behavioural thermoregulatory responses (Angilletta et al., 2019; Madden and Morrison, 2019; Siemens and Kamm, 2018; Tan and Knight, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The POA of various species of mammals contains neurons that respond to changes in local temperature.
source: The POA of various species of mammals also contains neurons that respond to changes in local temperature (Hardy et al., 1964; Hori et al., 1980a; Kelso et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation of POA neurons by cooling can occur in the absence of synaptic connections.
source: Activation of POA neurons by cooling can occur in the absence of synaptic connections and in vitro, suggesting a cell-autonomous mechanism of cold sensitivity (Abe et al., 2003; Hori et al., 1980b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation of POA neurons by cooling can occur in vitro.
source: Activation of POA neurons by cooling can occur in the absence of synaptic connections and in vitro, suggesting a cell-autonomous mechanism of cold sensitivity (Abe et al., 2003; Hori et al., 1980b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cold sensitivity of POA neurons involves a cell-autonomous mechanism.
source: Activation of POA neurons by cooling can occur in the absence of synaptic connections and in vitro, suggesting a cell-autonomous mechanism of cold sensitivity (Abe et al., 2003; Hori et al., 1980b).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cooling activates POA neurons in the absence of synaptic connections and in vitro.

claim: Cold-sensing POA neurons are thought to contribute to the feedback thermoregulatory pathway by directly responding to changes in intracranial temperature.
source: Although the physiological role of cold-sensing neurons remains obscure, they are thought to contribute, together with warm-sensing POA neurons, to the feedback thermoregulatory pathway by directly responding to changes in intracranial temperature (Madden and Morrison, 2019; Siemens and Kamm, 2018; Tan and Knight, 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cold-sensitive POA neurons are found in fish, reptiles, and birds.
source: Cold-sensitive POA neurons are found not only in mammals, but also in fish, reptiles and birds, suggesting an ancient origin and evolutionary conservation of this process (Cabanac et al., 1967; Nelson and Prosser, 1981; Simon et al., 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The presence of cold-sensitive POA neurons in fish, reptiles, birds, and mammals suggests an ancient origin and evolutionary conservation of this process.
source: Cold-sensitive POA neurons are found not only in mammals, but also in fish, reptiles and birds, suggesting an ancient origin and evolutionary conservation of this process (Cabanac et al., 1967; Nelson and Prosser, 1981; Simon et al., 1977).
evidence: This is inferred from the widespread presence of cold-sensitive POA neurons across vertebrate taxa.

claim: 10.0 ± 0.9% of dissociated mouse POA neurons responded to cooling.
source: Using ratiometric calcium imaging, we found that 10.0 ± 0.9% of dissociated mouse POA neurons responded to cooling (Figure 1A–C), consistent with previous studies (Abe et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The proportion of cold-sensitive POA neurons in mice is consistent with previous studies.
source: Using ratiometric calcium imaging, we found that 10.0 ± 0.9% of dissociated mouse POA neurons responded to cooling (Figure 1A–C), consistent with previous studies (Abe et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Active squirrels contained 6.8 ± 0.8% cold-activated POA neurons.
source: In contrast, active squirrels contained a significantly smaller population of cold-activated POA neurons (6.8 ± 0.8%, p<0.05 vs. mice, Mann-Whitney test, Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The proportion of cold-activated POA neurons in active squirrels is significantly smaller than in mice (p<0.05).
source: In contrast, active squirrels contained a significantly smaller population of cold-activated POA neurons (6.8 ± 0.8%, p<0.05 vs. mice, Mann-Whitney test, Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental calcium imaging data.

claim: The proportion of warm-sensitive cells was similar in both mouse and squirrel POA.
source: The difference was specific to cold-sensing neurons because the proportion of warm-sensitive cells was similar in both mouse and squirrel POA (mice: 15.2 ± 3.7%, squirrels: 15.1 ± 3.1%, p>0.05, Mann-Whitney test, Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The difference in cold-sensitive neurons between mice and squirrels is specific to cold-sensing neurons.
source: The difference was specific to cold-sensing neurons because the proportion of warm-sensitive cells was similar in both mouse and squirrel POA (mice: 15.2 ± 3.7%, squirrels: 15.1 ± 3.1%, p>0.05, Mann-Whitney test, Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that warm-sensitive cell proportions are similar while cold-sensitive proportions differ.

claim: A population of mouse POA neurons might possess a cold-sensing mechanism that is absent in squirrel POA.
source: These data suggest that a population of mouse POA neurons might possess a cold-sensing mechanism that is absent in squirrel POA.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in proportions of cold-sensitive neurons between mice and squirrels.

claim: Cnga3 was the most highly enriched transcript within the cold-sensitive neuronal population (14-fold enrichment).
source: Transcriptome analysis of pooled cold-sensitive versus cold-insensitive mouse POA neurons revealed that the most highly enriched transcript within the cold-sensitive neuronal population was the cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channel Cnga3 (14-fold enrichment, Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 2.

claim: RNA in situ hybridization confirmed the expression of Cnga3 in a subset of mouse POA neurons.
source: RNA in situ hybridization confirmed the expression of Cnga3 in a subset of mouse POA neurons (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Mice contain a population of cold-sensitive POA neurons which are enriched with CNGA3 channels.
source: Together, these data reveal that mice contain a population of cold-sensitive POA neurons, which are enriched with CNGA3 channels.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic and RNA in situ hybridization data.

claim: Injection of cGMP into the POA alters the firing rate and thermosensitivity of hypothalamic neurons.
source: This idea is supported by the findings that injection of the endogenous cyclic nucleotide-gated channel activator, cGMP, into the POA alters the firing rate and thermosensitivity of hypothalamic neurons and affects core body temperature in several species (Wright et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Injection of cGMP into the POA affects core body temperature in several species.
source: This idea is supported by the findings that injection of the endogenous cyclic nucleotide-gated channel activator, cGMP, into the POA alters the firing rate and thermosensitivity of hypothalamic neurons and affects core body temperature in several species (Wright et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: l-cis-diltiazem drastically suppressed cold activation of mouse POA neurons.
source: Consistent with this, we found that l-cis-diltiazem, an inhibitor of CNGA3-containing heteromeric channels, drastically suppressed cold activation of mouse POA neurons (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental calcium imaging data presented in Figure 3.

claim: l-cis-diltiazem is an inhibitor of CNGA3-containing heteromeric channels.
source: Consistent with this, we found that l-cis-diltiazem, an inhibitor of CNGA3-containing heteromeric channels, drastically suppressed cold activation of mouse POA neurons (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the pharmacology of l-cis-diltiazem.

claim: l-cis-diltiazem failed to affect calcium influx in response to depolarization by high extracellular potassium.
source: At the same time, the inhibitor failed to affect calcium influx in response to depolarization by high extracellular potassium, demonstrating a specific effect on cold-sensing machinery (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental calcium imaging data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: l-cis-diltiazem has a specific effect on cold-sensing machinery.
source: At the same time, the inhibitor failed to affect calcium influx in response to depolarization by high extracellular potassium, demonstrating a specific effect on cold-sensing machinery (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that l-cis-diltiazem suppresses cold activation but not potassium-induced depolarization.

claim: l-cis-diltiazem failed to suppress activation of warm-sensitive cells.
source: Furthermore, the inhibitory effect of l-cis-diltiazem was specific to cold-sensing cells, as the drug failed to suppress activation of warm-sensitive cells (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental calcium imaging data presented in Figure 3D-F.

claim: The inhibitory effect of l-cis-diltiazem is specific to cold-sensing cells.
source: Furthermore, the inhibitory effect of l-cis-diltiazem was specific to cold-sensing cells, as the drug failed to suppress activation of warm-sensitive cells (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of l-cis-diltiazem on cold-sensitive versus warm-sensitive cells.

claim: CNGA3 is necessary for cold sensitivity of mouse POA neurons.
source: These data strongly indicate that CNGA3 is necessary for cold sensitivity of mouse POA neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological inhibition experiments with l-cis-diltiazem.

claim: Cooling from 22°C to 12°C failed to stimulate mCNGA3 in the absence of cGMP.
source: Cooling the extracellular solution from 22°C to 12°C failed to stimulate mCNGA3, demonstrating that cold alone does not activate the channel (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Xenopus oocytes presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Cold alone does not activate mCNGA3.
source: Cooling the extracellular solution from 22°C to 12°C failed to stimulate mCNGA3, demonstrating that cold alone does not activate the channel (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cooling without cGMP does not activate the channel.

claim: Cooling in the presence of 1 µM intracellular cGMP led to potent and reversible activation of mCNGA3 across a wide range of voltages (4-fold activation at 60 mV).
source: However, cooling in the presence of a sub-threshold concentration (1 µM) of intracellular cGMP led to potent and reversible activation of mCNGA3 across a wide range of voltages (4-fold activation at 60 mV), consistent with the idea that cold facilitates cGMP-mediated activation of the channel (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Xenopus oocytes presented in Figure 4B and D.

claim: Cold facilitates cGMP-mediated activation of mCNGA3.
source: However, cooling in the presence of a sub-threshold concentration (1 µM) of intracellular cGMP led to potent and reversible activation of mCNGA3 across a wide range of voltages (4-fold activation at 60 mV), consistent with the idea that cold facilitates cGMP-mediated activation of the channel (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cold potentiates mCNGA3 activity in the presence of sub-threshold cGMP.

claim: CNGA3 can co-assemble with CNGB1 or CNGB3 to form functional heteromeric channels.
source: CNGA3 can co-assemble with CNGB1 or CNGB3 to form functional heteromeric channels with increased sensitivity to inhibition by l-cis-diltiazem compared to CNGA3 homomers (Peng et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2003; Zhong et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CNGA3-CNGB1 or CNGA3-CNGB3 heteromeric channels have increased sensitivity to inhibition by l-cis-diltiazem compared to CNGA3 homomers.
source: CNGA3 can co-assemble with CNGB1 or CNGB3 to form functional heteromeric channels with increased sensitivity to inhibition by l-cis-diltiazem compared to CNGA3 homomers (Peng et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2003; Zhong et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The profound suppression of cold activation in the POA by l-cis-diltiazem suggests the presence of drug-sensitive heteromers.
source: The profound suppression of cold activation in the POA by l-cis-diltiazem suggests the presence of drug-sensitive heteromers.
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological properties of l-cis-diltiazem and the observed suppression of cold activation.

claim: Cngb1, but not Cngb3, is expressed in both cold-sensitive and insensitive POA neurons.
source: Our transcriptomic analysis revealed that Cngb1, but not Cngb3, is expressed in both cold-sensitive and insensitive POA neurons (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Co-expression of mCNGA3 with mCNGB1 led to a twofold inhibition of cold-activated current by l-cis-diltiazem compared to mCNGA3 alone.
source: Co-expression of mCNGA3 with mCNGB1 led to a twofold inhibition of cold-activated current by l-cis-diltiazem compared to mCNGA3 alone (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Xenopus oocytes presented in Figure 5B and C.

claim: CNGB1 cannot form functional homomers.
source: Since CNGB1 cannot form functional homomers, the drug-resistant fraction of the cold-activated current is likely due to the presence of mCNGA3 homomers (Zhong et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The drug-resistant fraction of the cold-activated current is likely due to the presence of mCNGA3 homomers.
source: Since CNGB1 cannot form functional homomers, the drug-resistant fraction of the cold-activated current is likely due to the presence of mCNGA3 homomers (Zhong et al., 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some cold-activated current remains after l-cis-diltiazem treatment and the knowledge that CNGB1 cannot form homomers.

claim: CNGA3-CNGB1 heteromers can form a cold-activated l-cis-diltiazem-sensitive ion channel.
source: Thus, CNGA3-CNGB1 heteromers can form a cold-activated l-cis-diltiazem-sensitive ion channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-expression experiments showing increased drug sensitivity.

claim: CNGA2 is a cGMP-activated ion channel.
source: To test if cold activates other members of the cyclic nucleotide-gated channel family, we analysed CNGA2, a cGMP-activated ion channel (Altenhofen et al., 1991; Gordon and Zagotta, 1995; Trudeau and Zagotta, 2003), which we found to be expressed in cold-activated and cold-insensitive mouse POA neurons at similar levels (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CNGA2 is expressed in cold-activated and cold-insensitive mouse POA neurons at similar levels.
source: To test if cold activates other members of the cyclic nucleotide-gated channel family, we analysed CNGA2, a cGMP-activated ion channel (Altenhofen et al., 1991; Gordon and Zagotta, 1995; Trudeau and Zagotta, 2003), which we found to be expressed in cold-activated and cold-insensitive mouse POA neurons at similar levels (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: Cold failed to activate mouse CNGA2 in oocytes in the presence of 1 µM intracellular cGMP.
source: In contrast to CNGA3, cold failed to activate mouse CNGA2 in oocytes in the presence of 1 µM intracellular cGMP (Figure 6B and C), while saturating 250 µM cGMP potently activated the channel (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Xenopus oocytes presented in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Saturating 250 µM cGMP potently activated mouse CNGA2.
source: In contrast to CNGA3, cold failed to activate mouse CNGA2 in oocytes in the presence of 1 µM intracellular cGMP (Figure 6B and C), while saturating 250 µM cGMP potently activated the channel (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Xenopus oocytes presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Cold activation is specific to CNGA3 among the cyclic nucleotide-gated channel family.
source: This result demonstrates that cold activation is specific to CNGA3 among the cyclic nucleotide-gated channel family.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cold activates CNGA3 but not CNGA2.

claim: Cold failed to potentiate the activity of Cnga3 cloned from squirrel POA (sqCNGA3).
source: Strikingly, cold failed to potentiate the activity of Cnga3 cloned from squirrel POA (sqCNGA3, Figure 4C and D), even though activation with a saturating 250 µM cGMP revealed that sqCNGA3 was abundantly expressed on the surface of the oocytes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Xenopus oocytes presented in Figure 4C and D.

claim: sqCNGA3 was abundantly expressed on the surface of the oocytes.
source: Strikingly, cold failed to potentiate the activity of Cnga3 cloned from squirrel POA (sqCNGA3, Figure 4C and D), even though activation with a saturating 250 µM cGMP revealed that sqCNGA3 was abundantly expressed on the surface of the oocytes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing robust currents with saturating cGMP, presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Cooling from 22°C to 12°C reversibly potentiated mouse CNGA3 at positive and negative potentials in the presence of 2 µM cGMP in HEK293T cells.
source: In agreement with the data from oocytes, cooling from 22°C to 12°C reversibly potentiated mouse CNGA3 at positive and negative potentials in the presence of a sub-threshold 2 µM cGMP, but failed to affect squirrel CNGA3 (Figure 7A–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1), even though both channels were abundantly expressed on the plasma membrane, as revealed by recordings in the presence of saturating 100 µM intracellular cGMP (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in HEK293T cells presented in Figure 7.

claim: Cooling from 22°C to 12°C failed to affect squirrel CNGA3 in HEK293T cells in the presence of 2 µM cGMP.
source: In agreement with the data from oocytes, cooling from 22°C to 12°C reversibly potentiated mouse CNGA3 at positive and negative potentials in the presence of a sub-threshold 2 µM cGMP, but failed to affect squirrel CNGA3 (Figure 7A–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1), even though both channels were abundantly expressed on the plasma membrane, as revealed by recordings in the presence of saturating 100 µM intracellular cGMP (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in HEK293T cells presented in Figure 7.

claim: Both mouse and squirrel CNGA3 were abundantly expressed on the plasma membrane of HEK293T cells.
source: In agreement with the data from oocytes, cooling from 22°C to 12°C reversibly potentiated mouse CNGA3 at positive and negative potentials in the presence of a sub-threshold 2 µM cGMP, but failed to affect squirrel CNGA3 (Figure 7A–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1), even though both channels were abundantly expressed on the plasma membrane, as revealed by recordings in the presence of saturating 100 µM intracellular cGMP (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing robust currents with saturating cGMP, presented in Figure 7E and F.

claim: Cooling led to a robust activation of mCNGA3, with an apparent temperature threshold of 22.4 ± 0.8°C.
source: Cooling led to a robust activation of mCNGA3, with an apparent temperature threshold of 22.4 ± 0.8°C, and a 10-degree activation coefficient (Q10) of 6.5 ± 0.5 (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Xenopus oocytes presented in Figure 8.

claim: mCNGA3 has a 10-degree activation coefficient (Q10) of 6.5 ± 0.5.
source: Cooling led to a robust activation of mCNGA3, with an apparent temperature threshold of 22.4 ± 0.8°C, and a 10-degree activation coefficient (Q10) of 6.5 ± 0.5 (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in Xenopus oocytes presented in Figure 8.

claim: Cold specifically and reversibly potentiates the activity of mouse, but not squirrel CNGA3 in the presence of subthreshold intracellular cGMP.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that cold specifically and reversibly potentiates the activity of mouse, but not squirrel CNGA3 in the presence of subthreshold intracellular cGMP, and that this effect is independent of cell type.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in multiple cell types.

claim: The cold potentiation effect on mouse CNGA3 is independent of cell type.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that cold specifically and reversibly potentiates the activity of mouse, but not squirrel CNGA3 in the presence of subthreshold intracellular cGMP, and that this effect is independent of cell type.
evidence: This is supported by observations in both Xenopus oocytes and HEK293T cells.

claim: Cold sensitivity of mouse POA neurons is mediated by heteromers and homomers of CNGA3.
source: Our results also agree with the notion that cold sensitivity of mouse POA neurons is mediated by heteromers and homomers of CNGA3.
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological and electrophysiological data.

claim: Cooling from 21.8 ± 5.48 µM at 22°C to 3.5 ± 0.63 µM at 12°C significantly decreased the half-maximal cGMP concentration (EC50) for mouse CNGA3.
source: Paired recordings from the same patches at different temperatures revealed a significant decrease in half-maximal cGMP concentration (EC50) upon cooling from 21.8 ± 5.48 µM at 22°C to 3.5 ± 0.63 µM at 12°C (Figure 9C and E).
evidence: This is supported by inside-out patch recordings in HEK293T cells presented in Figure 9.

claim: There was no significant change in cGMP EC50 for squirrel CNGA3 upon cooling (26.4 ± 1.12 µM at 22°C, 20.4 ± 2.14 µM at 12°C).
source: In contrast to mouse CNGA3, and in agreement with our whole-cell data in oocytes and HEK293T cells, we did not detected a significant change in cGMP EC50 for squirrel CNGA3 (26.4 ± 1.12 µM at 22°C, 20.4 ± 2.14 µM at 12°C, Figure 9B,D and E).
evidence: This is supported by inside-out patch recordings in HEK293T cells presented in Figure 9.

claim: Cooling from 22°C to 12°C at saturating (≥100 µM) cGMP concentrations inhibited maximal activity of mouse CNGA3 by 25%.
source: Interestingly, cooling from 22°C to 12°C at saturating (≥100 µM) cGMP concentrations inhibited maximal activity of mouse CNGA3 by 25%, whereas this effect was significantly higher for the squirrel channel (60%, Figure 9F).
evidence: This is supported by inside-out patch recordings in HEK293T cells presented in Figure 9F.

claim: Cooling from 22°C to 12°C at saturating (≥100 µM) cGMP concentrations inhibited maximal activity of squirrel CNGA3 by 60%.
source: Interestingly, cooling from 22°C to 12°C at saturating (≥100 µM) cGMP concentrations inhibited maximal activity of mouse CNGA3 by 25%, whereas this effect was significantly higher for the squirrel channel (60%, Figure 9F).
evidence: This is supported by inside-out patch recordings in HEK293T cells presented in Figure 9F.

claim: The potentiating effect of cold at low cGMP concentrations is specific to mouse CNGA3.
source: Together, these findings reveal that the potentiating effect of cold at low cGMP concentrations is specific to mouse CNGA3, and is caused by a decrease in EC50 for the cyclic nucleotide.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of cold on mouse versus squirrel CNGA3 EC50.

claim: The potentiating effect of cold on mouse CNGA3 is caused by a decrease in EC50 for cGMP.
source: Together, these findings reveal that the potentiating effect of cold at low cGMP concentrations is specific to mouse CNGA3, and is caused by a decrease in EC50 for the cyclic nucleotide.
evidence: This is supported by the inside-out patch recordings showing decreased EC50 with cooling.

claim: Cold may act by enhancing the affinity between CNGA3 and cGMP.
source: We established that cold decreases the effective concentration of cGMP needed for mouse CNGA3 activation, suggesting that it acts by enhancing the affinity between the channel and the nucleotide and/or facilitating channel opening in response to nucleotide binding (James and Zagotta, 2018).
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed decrease in EC50 and cited literature.

claim: Cold may act by facilitating channel opening in response to nucleotide binding.
source: We established that cold decreases the effective concentration of cGMP needed for mouse CNGA3 activation, suggesting that it acts by enhancing the affinity between the channel and the nucleotide and/or facilitating channel opening in response to nucleotide binding (James and Zagotta, 2018).
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed decrease in EC50 and cited literature.

claim: The mechanism of cold activation of mouse CNGA3 is intrinsic to the channel and does not involve cell type-specific components.
source: The observation that cold activates mouse CNGA3 in various cell types strongly suggests that this mechanism is intrinsic to the channel and does not involve cell type-specific components.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cold activates mouse CNGA3 in multiple cell types.

claim: Cold acts on mouse CNGA3 even in inside-out patches.
source: Furthermore, our finding that cold acts on mouse CNGA3 even in inside-out patches, and fails to increase activity of mouse CNGA2 and the squirrel orthologue of CNGA3 argues against the involvement of indirect pathways such as cold-induced augmentation of cGMP production (Chao et al., 2015; Mamasuew et al., 2010; Stebe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by inside-out patch recordings.

claim: Cold fails to increase activity of mouse CNGA2.
source: Furthermore, our finding that cold acts on mouse CNGA3 even in inside-out patches, and fails to increase activity of mouse CNGA2 and the squirrel orthologue of CNGA3 argues against the involvement of indirect pathways such as cold-induced augmentation of cGMP production (Chao et al., 2015; Mamasuew et al., 2010; Stebe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The cold sensitivity of mouse CNGA3 does not involve indirect pathways such as cold-induced augmentation of cGMP production.
source: Furthermore, our finding that cold acts on mouse CNGA3 even in inside-out patches, and fails to increase activity of mouse CNGA2 and the squirrel orthologue of CNGA3 argues against the involvement of indirect pathways such as cold-induced augmentation of cGMP production (Chao et al., 2015; Mamasuew et al., 2010; Stebe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the observations in inside-out patches and the specificity of cold effects.

claim: The cyclic nucleotide gated ion channel Tax-4 is expressed in thermosensory neurons in C. elegans.
source: A study in C. elegans showed that the cyclic nucleotide gated ion channel Tax-4 is expressed in thermosensory neurons, and that tax-4 mutants exhibit aberrant thermotaxic behavior, suggesting that thermosensitivity of mouse CNGA3 may have a deep evolutionary origin (Komatsu et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: tax-4 mutants in C. elegans exhibit aberrant thermotaxic behavior.
source: A study in C. elegans showed that the cyclic nucleotide gated ion channel Tax-4 is expressed in thermosensory neurons, and that tax-4 mutants exhibit aberrant thermotaxic behavior, suggesting that thermosensitivity of mouse CNGA3 may have a deep evolutionary origin (Komatsu et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Thermosensitivity of mouse CNGA3 may have a deep evolutionary origin.
source: A study in C. elegans showed that the cyclic nucleotide gated ion channel Tax-4 is expressed in thermosensory neurons, and that tax-4 mutants exhibit aberrant thermotaxic behavior, suggesting that thermosensitivity of mouse CNGA3 may have a deep evolutionary origin (Komatsu et al., 1996).
evidence: This is speculated based on the similarity to C. elegans Tax-4.

claim: The strong correspondence between the proportion of cold-sensitive POA neurons and cold sensitivity of CNGA3 in both mice and squirrels suggests that the channel could be important for the detection of cold temperatures in the POA.
source: The strong correspondence between the proportion of cold-sensitive POA neurons and cold sensitivity of CNGA3 in both mice and squirrels suggests that the channel could be important for the detection of cold temperatures in the POA.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between neuronal cold sensitivity and CNGA3 cold sensitivity across species.

claim: In mice, the CNGA3-expressing cold-sensitive neurons could be a part of the mechanism that orchestrates thermogenesis in response to body cooling.
source: A tantalizing possibility is that in mice the CNGA3-expressing cold-sensitive neurons could be a part of the mechanism that orchestrates thermogenesis in response to body cooling.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential physiological role of CNGA3-expressing neurons.

claim: In squirrels, the thermogenic mechanism is expected to be inhibited to allow for the profound drop of core body temperature during transition into torpor.
source: In squirrels such mechanism is expected to be inhibited to allow for the profound drop of core body temperature during transition into torpor.
evidence: This is inferred from the known physiology of hibernating squirrels.

claim: A small fraction of squirrel POA neurons exhibits cold sensitivity.
source: Our observation that a small fraction of squirrel POA neurons exhibits cold sensitivity suggests the presence of a CNGA3-independent mechanism, which could be important for active monitoring of body temperature during hibernation (Andrews, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: The presence of cold-sensitive neurons in squirrels suggests a CNGA3-independent mechanism.
source: Our observation that a small fraction of squirrel POA neurons exhibits cold sensitivity suggests the presence of a CNGA3-independent mechanism, which could be important for active monitoring of body temperature during hibernation (Andrews, 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that squirrels have cold-sensitive neurons despite having cold-insensitive CNGA3.

claim: A CNGA3-independent cold-sensing mechanism could be important for active monitoring of body temperature during hibernation.
source: Our observation that a small fraction of squirrel POA neurons exhibits cold sensitivity suggests the presence of a CNGA3-independent mechanism, which could be important for active monitoring of body temperature during hibernation (Andrews, 2019).
evidence: This is speculation about the potential role of CNGA3-independent cold-sensitive neurons in squirrels.

claim: The CNGA3 sensor likely exists in POA neurons not only as a homomer, but also as a heteromer with CNGB1.
source: Our data suggest that the CNGA3 sensor likely exists in POA neurons not only as a homomer, but also as a heteromer with CNGB1 (Dai et al., 2013; Peng et al., 2004; Zhong et al., 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological data and expression of CNGB1 in POA neurons.

claim: The apparent activation threshold for homomeric CNGA3 is lower than the physiological brain temperature.
source: Although the apparent activation threshold for homomeric CNGA3 is lower than the physiological brain temperature, it may depend on the cellular environment and recording conditions, similar to other thermo-sensitive channels (Hoffstaetter et al., 2018; Song et al., 2016; Tan and McNaughton, 2016; Tominaga et al., 1998).
evidence: This is acknowledged based on the experimental data and cited literature on other thermosensitive channels.

claim: The temperature sensitivity of hypothalamic neurons is plastic and is modulated by metabolic state, circadian cycle, oxygenation, inflammatory status and peripheral nutrient signals.
source: The temperature sensitivity of hypothalamic neurons is plastic and is modulated by metabolic state, circadian cycle, oxygenation, inflammatory status and peripheral nutrient signals (Bartfai and Conti, 2012; Glotzbach and Heller, 1984; Pierau et al., 1998; Tattersall and Milsom, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The impact of CNGA3 on neuronal excitability will depend on the level of expression, neuronal resistance, and other cellular properties.
source: In addition, the impact of CNGA3 on neuronal excitability will depend on the level of expression, neuronal resistance, and other cellular properties.
evidence: This is inferred from general principles of neuronal physiology.

claim: CNGA3 is a major cGMP-activated depolarizing ion channel in the cone photoreceptors.
source: CNGA3 is best known for its role as a major cGMP-activated depolarizing ion channel in the cone photoreceptors (Bönigk et al., 1993; Cukkemane et al., 2011; Dai et al., 2013; Kaupp and Seifert, 2002; Peng et al., 2004; Yu et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CNGA3 is implicated in the cold modulation of olfactory neurons in the Grueneberg ganglion.
source: The channel is also implicated in the cold modulation of olfactory neurons in the Grueneberg ganglion, and is enriched in a subpopulation of peripheral cold receptors from dorsal root ganglia (Luiz et al., 2019; Mamasuew et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CNGA3 is enriched in a subpopulation of peripheral cold receptors from dorsal root ganglia.
source: The channel is also implicated in the cold modulation of olfactory neurons in the Grueneberg ganglion, and is enriched in a subpopulation of peripheral cold receptors from dorsal root ganglia (Luiz et al., 2019; Mamasuew et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CNGA3 is expressed in the amygdala and hippocampus.
source: Additionally, CNGA3 is expressed in the amygdala and hippocampus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CNGA3 expression.

claim: A global deletion of Cnga3 causes color blindness.
source: Consistent with the expression pattern, a global deletion of Cnga3 causes color blindness, affects odor recognition and produces deficits in hippocampal plasticity and amygdala-dependent fear memory (Biel et al., 1999; Leinders-Zufall et al., 2007; Michalakis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A global deletion of Cnga3 affects odor recognition.
source: Consistent with the expression pattern, a global deletion of Cnga3 causes color blindness, affects odor recognition and produces deficits in hippocampal plasticity and amygdala-dependent fear memory (Biel et al., 1999; Leinders-Zufall et al., 2007; Michalakis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A global deletion of Cnga3 produces deficits in hippocampal plasticity.
source: Consistent with the expression pattern, a global deletion of Cnga3 causes color blindness, affects odor recognition and produces deficits in hippocampal plasticity and amygdala-dependent fear memory (Biel et al., 1999; Leinders-Zufall et al., 2007; Michalakis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A global deletion of Cnga3 produces deficits in amygdala-dependent fear memory.
source: Consistent with the expression pattern, a global deletion of Cnga3 causes color blindness, affects odor recognition and produces deficits in hippocampal plasticity and amygdala-dependent fear memory (Biel et al., 1999; Leinders-Zufall et al., 2007; Michalakis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Further understanding of the role of CNGA3 in thermoregulation would require a conditional ablation of the channel in the POA of adult mice.
source: Given the complex phenotype of whole-body Cnga3 knock-out animals, further understanding of the role of CNGA3 in thermoregulation would require a conditional ablation of the channel in the POA of adult mice and/or a targeted disruption of cold-sensing capability of CNGA3 while preserving its function as a cGMP sensor.
evidence: This is speculation about future experimental approaches.
